# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

## The task
Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.

Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.

## What to submit
This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| README.md | Setup, supported runtime/provider, exact intake/test/accuracy-check commands, environment-variable names, and how to inspect the queue |
| Source code and dependency lockfile | Runnable application, extraction prompt, schema and model request configuration |
| deliverables/extractions.jsonl | One current record per message: document_id, source_sha256, extraction (schema-conforming object, or null on error), status, owner, next_action, error (null on success), and response_source (`mock`, or the provider and model ID that produced the record) |
| deliverables/queue.json | The review queue linked to extraction records by document_id |
| deliverables/accuracy.md | Source-derived expected fields for the 20 supplied messages and one paraphrase you author; the field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules, factual-error reporting and model/configuration; distinguish mocked examples from any optional live observations |
| deliverables/request-evidence.json | Credential-redacted example model request showing the model ID and configuration used, plus the implemented response handling |
| deliverables/verification.md | Verification commands and assertions, their intended comparisons, operating limits, and any observed results or repairs clearly identified as such |
| Coding-session capture | Session record paired with the submitted commit, collected through the facilitator's capture setup |

## Submission
Commit and push the application, outputs and session capture to your repository's default branch. Submit only the root repository link (`https://github.com/<your-account>/<repository>`) through the Classroom assignment. The facilitator supplies the assignment and capture instructions.

Submit the implemented provider integration and source-grounded validation procedure. Use mocked responses for reproducible development examples, and label each recorded observation with its configuration and whether it used a mock or provider response. The committed deliverables may come from mocked or provider responses; each record's response_source says which.
# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior
- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.

## Verification

Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.


Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.
# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.

# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

## The task
Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.

Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.

## What to submit
This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| README.md | Setup, supported runtime/provider, exact intake/test/accuracy-check commands, environment-variable names, and how to inspect the queue |
| Source code and dependency lockfile | Runnable application, extraction prompt, schema and model request configuration |
| deliverables/extractions.jsonl | One current record per message: document_id, source_sha256, extraction (schema-conforming object, or null on error), status, owner, next_action, error (null on success), and response_source (`mock`, or the provider and model ID that produced the record) |
| deliverables/queue.json | The review queue linked to extraction records by document_id |
| deliverables/accuracy.md | Source-derived expected fields for the 20 supplied messages and one paraphrase you author; the field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules, factual-error reporting and model/configuration; distinguish mocked examples from any optional live observations |
| deliverables/request-evidence.json | Credential-redacted example model request showing the model ID and configuration used, plus the implemented response handling |
| deliverables/verification.md | Verification commands and assertions, their intended comparisons, operating limits, and any observed results or repairs clearly identified as such |
| Coding-session capture | Session record paired with the submitted commit, collected through the facilitator's capture setup |

## Submission
Commit and push the application, outputs and session capture to your repository's default branch. Submit only the root repository link (`https://github.com/<your-account>/<repository>`) through the Classroom assignment. The facilitator supplies the assignment and capture instructions.

Submit the implemented provider integration and source-grounded validation procedure. Use mocked responses for reproducible development examples, and label each recorded observation with its configuration and whether it used a mock or provider response. The committed deliverables may come from mocked or provider responses; each record's response_source says which.
# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior
- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.

## Verification

Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.


Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.
# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.

1	# Northstar access-request intake policy
     2	
     3	Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.
     4	
     5	## Input export format
     6	Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.
     7	
     8	Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.
     9	
    10	## Extracted facts
    11	Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.
    12	
    13	Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.
    14	
    15	The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.
    16	
    17	## Review queue
    18	Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:
    19	
    20	1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
    21	2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
    22	3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
    23	4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
    24	5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.
    25	
    26	All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.
    27	
    28	## Processing and recovery
    29	An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.
    30	
    31	Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.

1	# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests
     2	
     3	## The task
     4	Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.
     5	
     6	Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.
     7	
     8	## What to submit
     9	This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.
    10	
    11	| Path | Content |
    12	|---|---|
    13	| README.md | Setup, supported runtime/provider, exact intake/test/accuracy-check commands, environment-variable names, and how to inspect the queue |
    14	| Source code and dependency lockfile | Runnable application, extraction prompt, schema and model request configuration |
    15	| deliverables/extractions.jsonl | One current record per message: document_id, source_sha256, extraction (schema-conforming object, or null on error), status, owner, next_action, error (null on success), and response_source (`mock`, or the provider and model ID that produced the record) |
    16	| deliverables/queue.json | The review queue linked to extraction records by document_id |
    17	| deliverables/accuracy.md | Source-derived expected fields for the 20 supplied messages and one paraphrase you author; the field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules, factual-error reporting and model/configuration; distinguish mocked examples from any optional live observations |
    18	| deliverables/request-evidence.json | Credential-redacted example model request showing the model ID and configuration used, plus the implemented response handling |
    19	| deliverables/verification.md | Verification commands and assertions, their intended comparisons, operating limits, and any observed results or repairs clearly identified as such |
    20	| Coding-session capture | Session record paired with the submitted commit, collected through the facilitator's capture setup |
    21	
    22	## Submission
    23	Commit and push the application, outputs and session capture to your repository's default branch. Submit only the root repository link (`https://github.com/<your-account>/<repository>`) through the Classroom assignment. The facilitator supplies the assignment and capture instructions.
    24	
    25	Submit the implemented provider integration and source-grounded validation procedure. Use mocked responses for reproducible development examples, and label each recorded observation with its configuration and whether it used a mock or provider response. The committed deliverables may come from mocked or provider responses; each record's response_source says which.

1	# Requirements — IT Access Requests
     2	
     3	## Operating context
     4	
     5	Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.
     6	
     7	### Workload and the review day
     8	
     9	On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.
    10	
    11	Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.
    12	
    13	### Shared operations
    14	
    15	Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.
    16	
    17	The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.
    18	
    19	### Updates and follow-up
    20	
    21	Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.
    22	
    23	Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.
    24	
    25	The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.
    26	
    27	### Service interruptions and handover
    28	
    29	The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.
    30	
    31	The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.
    32	
    33	## Record and review behavior
    34	- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
    35	- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
    36	- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
    37	- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
    38	- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
    39	- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.
    40	
    41	## Verification
    42	
    43	Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.
    44	
    45	
    46	Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.

content.text: Most gaps concern revision ordering, concurrent attempts, extraction semantics, and acceptance criteria. The policy does define routing precedence, raw-byte hashing and exact quote matching; the open questions are mainly how to classify inputs and handle cases around those rules. I also found places where `planning/spec.md` adopts an interpretation the sources don’t settle.

I found the following ambiguities and undefined terms. Some are deliberate implementation choices; others can change extraction, routing, recovery or acceptance results. I have left the files unchanged.

**Application scope and deliverables**

Source: [CHALLENGE.md — The task and What to submit](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/CHALLENGE.md:3).

| # | Wording or location | What remains open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | “small runnable application” | No supported operating system, resource budget or size limit is specified. |
| 2 | “interface suited to the IT team” | CLI, service and web are explicitly allowed, but suitability has no acceptance criteria. |
| 3 | “inspect completed results” | Required information, filtering, ordering and freshness of inspection are unspecified. |
| 4 | “review queue” | Its ordering, filtering and whether it includes errors or pending work are not fully defined. |
| 5 | `extractions.jsonl` fields | Types and structure of the outer record are unspecified; the supplied schema covers only `extraction`. |
| 6 | `response_source` | The representation of provider plus model ID is unspecified: string, object or another encoding. |
| 7 | `response_source` on failure | No value is defined when a provider never returns a response or no model call occurs. |
| 8 | `queue.json` | No JSON structure or complete required field list is supplied. |
| 9 | Linking by `document_id` | That identifies a document but not a particular source revision or attempt; the version-linking mechanism is unspecified. |
| 10 | “plus the implemented response handling” | `request-evidence.json` could contain a description, examples, code references or some combination. |
| 11 | “supported runtime/provider” | One supported configuration appears sufficient, but the required scope of compatibility is unstated. |
| 12 | “each recorded observation” | It is unclear which artifacts count as observations and how much configuration each label must include. |
| 13 | “repairs” | It is unclear whether this means code fixes, corrected extraction outputs, data repairs or all three. |
| 14 | “session record paired with the submitted commit” | Capture format, location and pairing mechanism depend on facilitator instructions outside these four files. |

**Workload, shared operation and recovery**

Source: [docs/requirements.md — Operating context](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/docs/requirements.md:7).

| # | Wording or location | What remains open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 15 | “200–400” daily and “roughly 2,000” morning messages | These establish workload context but no completion deadline, throughput or memory target. |
| 16 | “slow response” | No timeout or threshold distinguishes slow from failed. |
| 17 | “leave the rest of their work available” | This could mean completed results remain readable, other extractions keep progressing, or both. |
| 18 | Variable “request rate and response time” | Required rate controls, concurrency limits and adaptation behavior are unspecified. |
| 19 | Operators working against “the same” records | A shared process, shared filesystem and separate regional deployments imply different coordination requirements; deployment topology is unspecified. |
| 20 | “two operators may start processing around the same time” | Whether duplicate provider calls are acceptable is unstated, even if current outputs remain unique. |
| 21 | “coherent current queue” | Required consistency during concurrent writes is unspecified: for example, whether readers may temporarily see mixed revisions. |
| 22 | “trustworthy record of earlier activity” | Required audit events, metadata and protection against modification are unspecified. |
| 23 | “interrupted by a service outage” | The required interruption scope is unclear: process termination, machine failure, storage failure or model-service outage. |
| 24 | “completed” and “unfinished” | The durable completion boundary is unspecified: model response received, extraction persisted, queue persisted or all three. |
| 25 | “continue from the recorded state” | Recovery of work that was in flight is unspecified, including whether it may be called again. |
| 26 | “later export” and “latest processed source” | Latest could mean arrival order, export timestamp, processing start or processing completion. |
| 27 | Concurrent revisions | No winner is defined when an older revision finishes after a newer revision. |
| 28 | “current view” during refresh | It is unclear whether the prior result remains current while a replacement is pending, or whether pending replaces it. |
| 29 | “earlier results” and “earlier activity” | Retention duration, retention limits and whether every unsuccessful attempt must be retained are unspecified. |
| 30 | “relevant processing settings” | No definitive list identifies which settings invalidate reuse: model, prompt, schema, policy, temperature, provider endpoint or application version. |
| 31 | “refresh the affected results” | Automatic versus explicit refresh, selection of affected documents and whether policy-only changes require another model call are unspecified. |
| 32 | “policy version” | No version identifier or method for deriving one is supplied. |
| 33 | “unchanged” reuse after failure | It is unclear whether an unchanged failed attempt is reused, automatically retried or retried only through an explicit command. |
| 34 | “reproducible retry command” | Reproducibility could mean repeatable invocation or identical results; the settings and source version used by retry are unspecified. |

**Input format and document identity**

Source: [materials/office-policy.md — Input export format](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/materials/office-policy.md:5) and [Extracted facts](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/materials/office-policy.md:10).

| # | Wording or location | What remains open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 35 | Export format | No input schema defines required metadata, metadata types, supported `export_version` values or extra-field handling. |
| 36 | Invalid export | Behavior for invalid JSON, invalid UTF-8, missing/non-string `message` or an unreadable file is unspecified. |
| 37 | “up to 200 English words” | Word counting and behavior for longer or non-English messages are unspecified; this may describe the input domain rather than require rejection. |
| 38 | “filename” as `document_id` | Basename versus relative path, case sensitivity and collisions across directories are unspecified. |
| 39 | “identifier in its filename” | No parsing rule defines which filename substring is the request identifier. |
| 40 | Renamed files | A rename could create a new independent document or be treated as a revision; only content replacement under an existing identity is described. |
| 41 | “identifier inside the message” | Messages can contain several identifiers; selection of the request identifier versus incidental references is unspecified. |
| 42 | “one exported message” | A single message may contain several requests, systems or people, but the schema supports only one set of scalar facts. |

**Extraction meanings and schema boundaries**

Sources: [materials/office-policy.md — Extracted facts](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/materials/office-policy.md:10), [docs/requirements.md — Record and review behavior](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/docs/requirements.md:33), and [snapshot.schema.json](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/snapshot.schema.json:1).

| # | Wording or location | What remains open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 43 | `request_date` | It is not explicitly distinguished from a date of writing, submission or a prior request mentioned in the message. |
| 44 | `requester` | Sender, access beneficiary and person making a request on someone else’s behalf may differ. |
| 45 | `team` | Whether this means the requester’s team, beneficiary’s team or responsible system team is unstated. |
| 46 | `system` | Required granularity and normalization of aliases or abbreviations are unspecified. |
| 47 | `manager` | Whose manager is intended, and what identifying information is sufficient, are unspecified. |
| 48 | `business_purpose` | Verbatim extraction versus faithful summarization is not specified. |
| 49 | `kind` | The boundary between `other` and null is undefined; mixed new/change/withdrawal messages are not addressed. |
| 50 | Environment and permission vocabulary | Mapping phrases such as “prod,” “view access” or “read/write” into the enums is unspecified. |
| 51 | Unsupported environment or permission | Treatment of explicit values outside the enums is unspecified: null plus issue, `other` kind or extraction failure. |
| 52 | “explicit facts” | The permitted degree of inference, abbreviation expansion and normalization is undefined. |
| 53 | “uncertain” and “unresolved” | No confidence threshold or decision procedure defines when a field becomes null. |
| 54 | “missing” scalar | Empty strings, whitespace and placeholders satisfy the schema’s string type; their business treatment is unspecified. |
| 55 | “conflicting details” | The boundary between genuine contradiction, additional detail and compatible descriptions is undefined. |
| 56 | “explicitly labelled as a correction” | Accepted correction language, ordering across quoted/forwarded text and treatment of multiple corrections are unspecified. |
| 57 | Correction evidence | Whether superseded values must remain in supporting quotes or issues is unspecified. |
| 58 | “relative date” | The treatment of partly specified dates, weekdays, “immediately,” “ongoing” and dates relative to an explicit anchor is unstated. |
| 59 | Date normalization | Ambiguous numeric dates, omitted years, timestamps and timezone conversion are unspecified. |
| 60 | Date validity | Policy requires YYYY-MM-DD, but the schema checks neither that format nor actual calendar validity; failure versus clarification handling is unspecified. |
| 61 | Change requests | Only the requested new permission is explicitly addressed; interpretation of changes to system, environment, dates or other facts is unspecified. |
| 62 | `supporting_quotes` coverage | Exact substring matching is defined, but minimum evidence coverage, quote length, ordering and duplication rules are not. |
| 63 | `issues` representation | Free text versus structured conventions, per-field association, ordering and exact expected wording are unspecified. |
| 64 | Schema validation | No JSON Schema dialect is declared, and the boundary between structural validation failure and a business-fact issue is not fully defined. |

**Routing and human review**

Source: [materials/office-policy.md — Review queue](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/materials/office-policy.md:17).

| # | Wording or location | What remains open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 65 | “instruction-override attempt” | No classification boundary distinguishes malicious overrides from quoted examples, ordinary request instructions or harmless discussion. |
| 66 | Detecting overrides and other routing conditions | Responsibility between the model and deterministic application logic is unspecified; the schema has no dedicated override or conflict flags. |
| 67 | “source evidence” for an override | This could mean `supporting_quotes`, the retained original message or another artifact. |
| 68 | Validating extraction before override routing | If extraction fails on an override message, the relationship between the error route and override-review route is not expressly stated. |
| 69 | Withdrawal with ID and date | Ordered rules put this before mismatch/conflict checks, but what constitutes a usable ID/date when those fields are invalid or disputed remains open. |
| 70 | Incomplete withdrawal | The fallback required facts for a withdrawal missing ID or date are not explicitly listed; the required-fact list is limited to new/change requests. |
| 71 | “any missing required fact” | Kind is necessary for complete new/change routing but is excluded from the listed required facts; schema-required keys and business-required non-null facts must also be distinguished. |
| 72 | Other issues on otherwise complete requests | It is unspecified whether an issue outside the enumerated clarification conditions blocks complete-request routing. |
| 73 | “involving production, write or admin” | It is unclear whether only the extracted requested values count, or also existing access and incidental mentions in the message. |
| 74 | “named human reviewers” and “System Owner” | No person-to-system mapping or reviewer directory is supplied; literal team ownership versus assignment to an individual is unspecified. |
| 75 | Security review and forwarding | This can describe what humans do after intake or imply application-supported handoff; required workflow support is unspecified. |
| 76 | Withdrawal across documents | Documents are independent, but whether a withdrawal changes another document’s queue entry is not expressly stated. |

**Provider failures, storage and security**

Sources: [docs/requirements.md — Record and review behavior](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/docs/requirements.md:33) and [materials/office-policy.md — Processing and recovery](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/materials/office-policy.md:28).

| # | Wording or location | What remains open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 77 | “completion status,” “refusal” and “interrupted responses” | Required provider-specific signals and classification of partial text, truncation or mixed refusal/content are unspecified. |
| 78 | “handle … explicitly” | Automatic retries, retryable-error categories, retry limits, backoff and timeout behavior are unspecified. |
| 79 | “actionable error” | Required information and representation are undefined. |
| 80 | “extraction failure” | Whether this includes invalid input, missing configuration, persistence failure and routing failure is unspecified. |
| 81 | “prior versions separately” | Separate files/directories versus logically separate database records are both possible. |
| 82 | “last valid result” | Valid could mean structurally valid extraction or a fully persisted extraction-and-queue result. |
| 83 | Credential redaction | Credential categories and required redaction coverage across provider errors, URLs, headers and nested logs are unspecified. |

**Verification and acceptance**

Sources: [CHALLENGE.md — accuracy and verification deliverables](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/CHALLENGE.md:17) and [docs/requirements.md — Verification](/home/user/ai-full-stack-it-access-requests/docs/requirements.md:41).

| # | Wording or location | What remains open |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 84 | “expected fields” | Whether accuracy covers every extraction field, quote/issue arrays, routing fields or a selected subset is unspecified. |
| 85 | “exact-match counting/denominator rules” | The author must define them; nulls, failed extractions, array ordering, normalization and excluded fields have no prescribed treatment. |
| 86 | Accuracy acceptance | No minimum score or maximum factual-error count is specified. |
| 87 | “factual-error reporting” | Error categories, reporting unit and treatment of unsupported versus omitted facts are undefined. |
| 88 | “one paraphrase” / “paraphrased synthetic request” | Whether this must paraphrase one supplied message or may be an independently authored request is unclear. |
| 89 | “independently” constructed expectations | Required provenance and whether model-assisted expectation preparation is permitted are unspecified. |
| 90 | “refusal or interrupted responses” | The verification wording permits either, while behavior explicitly requires handling both; required test coverage is therefore open. |
| 91 | Operational checks | Minimum scenarios, scale and realism are unspecified; documentation of limits is expressly allowed. |
| 92 | Mocked versus live verification | Live observations are optional, but the required evidence for an implemented provider integration without a live run is unspecified. |

**Interpretations introduced in `planning/spec.md`**

These are places where my specification carries forward ambiguity or narrows the source wording:

| Spec row | Interpretation needing attention |
| --- | --- |
| R-05 | Its check verifies completed results remain inspectable; the source may also require other extractions to keep progressing. |
| R-06–R-08 | “Coherent,” “trustworthy” and version agreement remain without precise acceptance criteria. |
| R-12–R-13 | “Affected results,” relevant settings and policy-version representation remain undefined. |
| R-21–R-24 | Field presence is specified, but outer-record types and queue structure remain unspecified. |
| R-35 | Treats the 200-word statement as a supported input boundary; the source describes message length without defining validation behavior. |
| R-59 | A mocked exercise checks configuration plumbing but cannot by itself establish provider compatibility. |
| R-65 | “Supporting evidence” remains broader than a specifically named storage field. |
| R-73 | Adds inspection of queue/interface guidance for the security handoff; the source describes the human process without expressly requiring that guidance. |
| R-83 | Checking for a new retry attempt does not settle whether retry uses original or current source/settings. |
| R-88 | Retains the source’s “refusal or interrupted” coverage ambiguity. |
| R-90 | Requires documented assumptions but provides no objective workload acceptance threshold. |

description: Turns planning/spec.md into planning/plan.md before any code is written - ordered build steps, each naming the spec lines it meets and the test written first, with the test plan inside the plan. Use when asked to plan the build from the spec, or to write or fix the test plan.

# Plan from the spec

Write `planning/plan.md` from `planning/spec.md`. Write no application code and no tests in this
step: the plan is read and corrected by a person before anything is built.

## Read first

- `planning/spec.md`: the numbered requirements (R-01, R-02, ...) and how each is checked.
- `CHALLENGE.md`, `docs/requirements.md`, `materials/office-policy.md` and `snapshot.schema.json`:
  the sources the spec was written from.
- The request exports in `materials/requests/`: open the ones a test case uses, and read their
  `message` text.

## Write `planning/plan.md` with these four sections

1. **Choices.** The runtime, the interface (a CLI, a service or a web application), the test
   command, and how the model provider is called. One line each, with its reason.
2. **Steps, in build order.** A numbered list. Each step names the spec lines it meets
   (`R-03, R-07`), the test from the test plan that is written first and seen to fail, and what is
   true when the step is done. The first step builds the mock provider the tests use. Each test
   belongs to one step only, so every step has a test that fails until that step's code exists.
3. **Test plan.** A table, one row per case:

   | Case | Input | Mock response | Expected facts | Source of the expected facts | Spec lines |
   |---|---|---|---|---|---|

   - One row for each case in `docs/requirements.md` § Verification: a complete request, missing
     dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun and
     changed source content; then the paraphrased synthetic request, a refusal or interrupted
     response, and a failed retry after a prior success.
   - **Input** names the export file (or the new message you author) that shows the case. Find it by
     reading the messages.
   - **Mock response** says what the mock provider returns for that case: a reply saved under
     `tests/mock_responses/`, an error, or a cut-off reply. No test calls the real provider.
   - **Expected facts** are the field values, status, owner and next action the case must produce.
     Write them from the message text and the office policy, never from running the code.
   - **Source of the expected facts** quotes the words of the message and the policy rule they
     come from.
4. **Coverage.** Every spec line, each with the step that builds it and the test or check that
   shows it. A spec line with no step or no test is listed under "Not yet covered", with the reason.

## Before you finish

- Every spec line appears in § Coverage with a step and a test, or under "Not yet covered".
- Every expected fact has a quote from a message or the policy beside it.
- Every case of § Verification has its own row.
- No step and no test needs `API_KEY`.
- No test is named by two steps.

Where a spec line is unclear, say so in the plan and ask the person; do not guess a rule.

These questions record ambiguities and undefined terms; they do not add requirements or select answers. Some are implementation choices the files leave open. References to R-IDs identify related specification rows, including interpretations adopted by their checks.

Source abbreviations below: C = [CHALLENGE.md](../CHALLENGE.md); D = [docs/requirements.md](../docs/requirements.md); P = [materials/office-policy.md](../materials/office-policy.md); S = [snapshot.schema.json](../snapshot.schema.json).

# AI Full Stack Challenge — IT Access Requests

## The task
Northstar Labs receives access requests as free-text messages. Build a small runnable application that uses a language model to turn those messages into structured records and a review queue for the IT team. The supplied company, people and requests are fictional.

Read docs/requirements.md for the operating context and required behavior, materials/office-policy.md for review rules, and snapshot.schema.json for the record format. The 20 JSON exports in materials/requests/ are your starting data. Choose an interface suited to the IT team: a CLI, service or web application. Operators should be able to start intake, inspect completed results while other requests are pending, and resume unfinished work through the documented interface.

## What to submit
This brief ships as CHALLENGE.md; the README.md below is yours to write.

| Path | Content |
|---|---|
| README.md | Setup, supported runtime/provider, exact intake/test/accuracy-check commands, environment-variable names, and how to inspect the queue |
| Source code and dependency lockfile | Runnable application, extraction prompt, schema and model request configuration |
| deliverables/extractions.jsonl | One current record per message: document_id, source_sha256, extraction (schema-conforming object, or null on error), status, owner, next_action, error (null on success), and response_source (`mock`, or the provider and model ID that produced the record) |
| deliverables/queue.json | The review queue linked to extraction records by document_id |
| deliverables/accuracy.md | Source-derived expected fields for the 20 supplied messages and one paraphrase you author; the field-comparison procedure, exact-match counting/denominator rules, factual-error reporting and model/configuration; distinguish mocked examples from any optional live observations |
| deliverables/request-evidence.json | Credential-redacted example model request showing the model ID and configuration used, plus the implemented response handling |
| deliverables/verification.md | Verification commands and assertions, their intended comparisons, operating limits, and any observed results or repairs clearly identified as such |
| Coding-session capture | Session record paired with the submitted commit, collected through the facilitator's capture setup |

## Submission
Commit and push the application, outputs and session capture to your repository's default branch. Submit only the root repository link (`https://github.com/<your-account>/<repository>`) through the Classroom assignment. The facilitator supplies the assignment and capture instructions.

Submit the implemented provider integration and source-grounded validation procedure. Use mocked responses for reproducible development examples, and label each recorded observation with its configuration and whether it used a mock or provider response. The committed deliverables may come from mocked or provider responses; each record's response_source says which.
# Requirements — IT Access Requests

## Operating context

Northstar Labs is a fictional multinational company with approximately 5,000 employees across offices in Asia, Europe and North America. Its regional IT teams share responsibility for preparing access requests for human review. They receive free-text messages through email, chat and the service portal, then work from JSON exports of those messages.

### Workload and the review day

On an ordinary business day, the company receives around 200–400 request messages. A coordinated onboarding or acquisition can bring roughly 2,000 messages into the morning's intake. The supplied 20 exports are a representative sample of message types; the application will also receive other messages in the same export format.

Reviewers begin work at different local times. They want to start on requests that are ready while the rest of the intake is still being prepared. A slow response for one message should leave the rest of their work available. Model access is shared with other internal tools, and the available request rate and response time can vary.

### Shared operations

Regional operators work against the same intake and review records. Their working hours overlap, and two operators may start processing around the same time. Each expects their work to leave a coherent current queue and a trustworthy record of earlier activity.

The application may be stopped during a deployment or interrupted by a service outage. When an operator returns, they need to distinguish completed work from unfinished work and continue from the recorded state. Reviewers rely on the queue and the supporting extraction records agreeing about the same source version.

### Updates and follow-up

Exports arrive throughout the day. A later export may repeat an unchanged document or replace its contents with a corrected or expanded message. An export batch contains new or updated documents; absence from a later batch does not withdraw an earlier request. Withdrawal is expressed in the message and handled under the office policy.

Operators need the current view to reflect the latest processed source and to retain earlier results for follow-up. If a new processing attempt fails, they need to see that failure and identify any older result as belonging to its earlier attempt and source version.

The team periodically changes model configuration and updates its review policy. When such a change affects how records are produced or routed, operators need to refresh the affected results and understand which settings and policy version produced the records they are using.

### Service interruptions and handover

The model service sometimes responds slowly, limits requests or becomes temporarily unavailable. IT staff need to locate affected messages, understand what remains pending and resume processing without losing completed work. Other messages may contain incomplete or conflicting information that needs clarification from the requester.

The original developer and the next operator may be in different offices. The operator will use the repository's setup instructions, configuration guidance and commands to prepare an intake, inspect the queue and follow up on failures. Explain the operating assumptions and limits of your implementation so that this handover is practical.

## Record and review behavior
- Use a language model to extract the request details into records that conform to snapshot.schema.json.
- Validate response structure and completion status before using extracted data. Preserve exact supporting quotes and represent uncertain fields as null with an explanatory issue.
- Use message content as the source of business facts. Preserve missing values, conflicting alternatives and explicit corrections according to the policy. Keep document identity distinct from the request ID stated in the message.
- Apply the supplied review policy and display each request's status, owner and next action. Approval decisions belong to the named human reviewers.
- Record input filenames and SHA-256 hashes. Reuse results when the source and relevant processing settings are unchanged, refresh affected results when those inputs or settings change, and retain earlier versions. Process each message independently and make failures visible with a reproducible retry command.
- Handle malformed output, provider errors, refusal and interrupted responses explicitly. Keep model/provider settings configurable and document a supported configuration. The facilitator supplies an API key through the environment variable API_KEY.

## Verification

Include automated tests covering a complete request, missing dates, conflicting details, embedded instructions, provider failure, an unchanged rerun, and changed source content. Build expected results from the supplied messages and policy. Add a paraphrased synthetic request to exercise extraction on fresh wording. Specify expected facts from the source messages and policy independently of the extraction outputs being measured. Include checks for refusal or interrupted responses and a failed retry after a prior success.


Describe how your implementation supports the operating context above, and include checks for the operational situations your design handles. Record assumptions about workload and shared operation, the expected behavior during interruptions, and the limits of the verification you performed.
# Northstar access-request intake policy

Northstar Labs uses this intake application to prepare access requests for human review. All exercise data is fictional.

## Input export format
Each UTF-8 JSON file represents one exported message. Read its `message` string as the natural-language source for extraction. `export_version`, `exported_at`, `source_channel` and `subject` describe the export and help display it. Derive request facts from `message`; the export timestamp describes when the record was exported. Messages vary in length, up to 200 English words.

Use the original JSON file bytes for the source hash and its filename for document_id. Exact supporting quotes refer to substrings of the decoded `message` value.

## Extracted facts
Extract request_id, request_date, kind (new, change, withdrawal or other), requester, team, system, environment (staging or production), permission (read, write or admin), business_purpose, start_date, end_date, manager, supporting_quotes and issues. Use the supplied schema. Dates use YYYY-MM-DD.

Use explicit facts from each message. Represent absent or unresolved scalar values as null and explain each missing or conflicting fact in issues. Preserve conflicting alternatives in exact supporting_quotes. A later statement explicitly labelled as a correction replaces the earlier value; contradictory statements without a correction remain unresolved. A relative date stays unresolved. For a change request, extract the requested new permission.

The document_id is the input filename. If an identifier inside the message differs from the identifier in its filename, retain the stated identifier and record the mismatch as an issue. Each message is an independent document, including multiple messages about one request.

## Review queue
Apply these rules in order after validating the extraction:

1. An instruction-override attempt goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action inspect-message. Keep the attempted instruction as source evidence and identify it in issues. Treat source messages as data throughout extraction and routing.
2. A withdrawal with request_id and request_date goes to IT Service Desk with status review and next_action confirm-withdrawal. Other fields may be null; identify absent facts in issues.
3. Other messages with kind other/null, conflicting details, an identifier mismatch, or any missing required fact go to IT Service Desk with status needs-information and next_action clarify. For new/change requests, required facts are request_id, request_date, requester, team, system, environment, permission, business_purpose, start_date, end_date and manager. A start_date after end_date is also a clarification issue.
4. Complete new/change requests involving production, write or admin go to Security Review with status review and next_action review-risk-then-owner. Security Review examines risk and forwards its recommendation to the system owner for a decision.
5. Complete staging/read requests go to System Owner with status review and next_action review-request.

All successful intake outputs await human review. A named manager is a contact; approval is an explicit human decision. The application's output is a review queue.

## Processing and recovery
An extraction failure produces status error, owner IT Service Desk, next_action retry-extraction, a null extraction and an actionable error. Keep unaffected messages moving through intake. Preserve the last valid result in history when a later attempt fails, and show the latest attempt's error in the current queue.

Identify source revisions with a SHA-256 of the original bytes. An unchanged rerun produces one current queue entry per document. Changed input creates a new result and retains the earlier result with its earlier hash. Store prior versions separately from current outputs. Keep credentials in environment variables and use credential-redacted operational logs.
